claims.claim: Having a child with ADHD state one specific if-then plan ('If X happens, then I will do Y') before a task improved response inhibition in laboratory studies to the level of children without ADHD, so a single if-then plan at session start is a cheap, ADHD-tested tool.
claims.source_title: Implementation intentions facilitate response inhibition in children with ADHD
claims.url: NOT RETRIEVED - WebSearch budget exhausted before any search ran; verify by title
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran). Recalled, unverified: two small laboratory experiments with children diagnosed with ADHD, random assignment to a goal-intention vs if-then-plan condition on a go/no-go inhibition task; if-then planners' inhibition matched non-ADHD comparison children. General-population backdrop: Gollwitzer & Sheeran 2006 meta-analysis of implementation intentions, d about 0.65 across 94 tests.
claims.implication: The maths-tutor-session skill can script one if-then plan in the 10-minute starter, aimed at the logged failure modes: 'If I want to type skip, then I write down one thing I know'; 'If the question names one category, then I underline it before answering'; 'If I get an answer, then I write the working line first'. The plan should be in the student's own words, typed or said, and logged in the session summary so the next session reuses it.

claims.claim: If-then plans also improved delay of gratification and task-switching in children with ADHD, which supports using them for staying on a tedious practice question rather than jumping ahead or answering every part at once.
claims.source_title: If-then plans benefit delay of gratification performance in children with and without ADHD
claims.authors_year: Gawrilow, Gollwitzer & Oettingen, 2011 (Cognitive Therapy and Research)
claims.url: NOT RETRIEVED - WebSearch budget exhausted before any search ran; verify by title
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran). Recalled, unverified: children with and without ADHD randomised to goal-intention vs if-then-plan instructions on a delay-of-gratification task; if-then plans increased waiting in both groups. A companion 2011 paper by the same authors (Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, 'If-then plans benefit executive functions in children with ADHD') reported the same for task switching.
claims.implication: Frame the plan around the 'answer-targeting' and 'submit without working' habits: 'If I finish part (a), then I stop and check whether part (b) was actually asked'. Keep to one plan per session; the studies used a single concrete plan, not a list.

claims.claim: Self-monitoring (the student recording her own on-task behaviour or work completed at intervals) is the self-regulation tool with the largest and most consistent effects in ADHD samples, improving on-task behaviour, academic productivity and accuracy.
claims.source_title: Self-regulation interventions for children with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder
claims.url: NOT RETRIEVED - WebSearch budget exhausted before any search ran; verify by title
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran). Recalled, unverified: 16 studies, almost all single-subject designs, covering self-monitoring, self-monitoring plus reinforcement, self-management and self-reinforcement; large mean effects on on-task behaviour, academic productivity/accuracy and reductions in inappropriate behaviour. Samples were primary-age classroom pupils, not home-educated 13-year-olds.
claims.implication: The tracker records what Claude and the parent observe, never what the student observes about herself. Add a student self-check at the exit ticket (three yes/no ticks: showed working on every answer, read exactly what was asked, no blanks), store it on the practice run, and let the dashboard show her own tally next to the marker's. DuPaul & Stoner's 'self-monitoring with matching' variant (student rates, tutor rates, agreement is praised) is the classroom form of this and would fit the existing exit-ticket step.

claims.claim: A daily report card - three to five specific, observable, positively phrased targets with a daily pass criterion, reviewed the same day by the parent - improved classroom behaviour and academic productivity for children with ADHD in a randomised trial, but the tested version tied the review to home consequences.
claims.source_title: Enhancing the effectiveness of special education programming for children with ADHD using a daily report card
claims.url: NOT RETRIEVED - WebSearch budget exhausted before any search ran; verify by title
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran). Recalled, unverified: about 63 children with ADHD receiving special education, randomised to DRC vs business as usual over a school year; the DRC group showed better teacher-rated academic productivity, fewer observed rule violations and greater IEP goal progress; effect sizes not recalled.
claims.implication: The tracker already computes the best DRC-style target ('blanks per paper'). A session-end card with three targets (blanks = 0, working shown on every answer, answered only what was asked), reviewed by the parent the same day, copies the evidence-based structure. Note the tension with the README's no-rewards stance: the trial's card was tied to home privileges; a praise-and-review-only card is plausible but is not what was tested.

claims.claim: The HOPS programme (Homework, Organization and Planning Skills) for middle-school students with ADHD - materials checklists, writing every task in a planner, and breaking work into timed steps with a weekly parent check - produced large parent-rated improvements in organisation and homework problems in randomised trials, with much smaller teacher-rated change.
claims.source_title: Evaluation of the Homework, Organization, and Planning Skills (HOPS) intervention for middle school students with ADHD as implemented by school mental health providers
claims.authors_year: Langberg, Epstein, Becker, Girio-Herrera & Vaughn, 2012 (School Psychology Review, 41(3)); replicated at scale in Langberg et al., 2018 (Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, HOPS vs CHIEF)
claims.url: NOT RETRIEVED - WebSearch budget exhausted before any search ran; verify by title
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran). Recalled, unverified: 2012 trial about 47 students in grades 6-8 randomised to HOPS (16 brief school sessions plus two parent meetings) or waitlist; parent-rated organisation and homework-problem effects were large (roughly d about 1) and held at 3-month follow-up; teacher ratings did not differ significantly. 2018 trial about 280 students; both HOPS and CHIEF improved parent ratings, HOPS more on planning and organisation.
claims.implication: Translate HOPS to a home-educated setting: (1) one written weekly plan the student can see, listing each session's topic and planned minutes - today the 'planned next' list is Claude- and parent-facing only; (2) each practice task broken into steps with a minute estimate; (3) a weekly parent-student review of planned vs done. Expect gains in organisation and follow-through, not directly in grades.

claims.claim: Across randomised trials, organisational-skills training for children and adolescents with ADHD gives moderate improvements in organisation as rated by parents and teachers but only small improvements in inattention and academic performance, so planning tools should be expected to improve follow-through rather than exam grades.
claims.source_title: Meta-analysis of organizational skills interventions for children and adolescents with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
claims.authors_year: Bikic, Reichow, McCauley, Ibrahim & Sukhodolsky, 2017 (Clinical Psychology Review, 52)
claims.url: NOT RETRIEVED - WebSearch budget exhausted before any search ran; verify by title

claims.implication: Keep retrieval practice and marked papers as the grade lever; use planning tools to protect session completion (the 'Q4/Q5 not submitted before the session ended' pattern) and do not read a tidy planner as evidence of maths progress. Progress reports should keep the two apart: coverage and attempt grades on one line, follow-through metrics on another.

claims.source_title: Evidence-based psychosocial treatments for children and adolescents with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder

That ordering should decide which features are built first.

claims.claim: Children and young adults with ADHD are measurably worse at judging and reproducing elapsed time, especially for longer intervals and under distraction, which is the basis for Barkley's advice to make time external and visible rather than relying on the student's sense of it.
claims.source_title: Sense of time in children with ADHD: effects of duration, distraction, and stimulant medication
claims.authors_year: Barkley, Koplowitz, Anderson & McMurray, 1997 (Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society); extended in Barkley, Murphy & Bush, 2001 (Neuropsychology, 'Time perception and reproduction in young adults with ADHD')
claims.url: NOT RETRIEVED - WebSearch budget exhausted before any search ran; verify by title
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran). Recalled, unverified: case-control laboratory time-reproduction tasks at 12 to 60 seconds; the ADHD group's reproductions were less accurate at longer durations and worsened with distraction; medication partly helped. The 2001 young-adult study found under-reproduction of longer intervals.
claims.implication: The 90-minute session shape should not assume she can feel where she is in it. Have the tutor announce time at every block boundary ('30 minutes left, two questions to go'), log actual session length and whether it ended finished or ran out (neither is recorded today), and show remaining time on screen during timed practice.

claims.claim: People in general predict task completion times that are far too short (the planning fallacy), and this has been measured in students, so any weekly plan built from the student's own time estimates will be optimistic unless estimates are checked against logged actuals.
claims.source_title: Exploring the 'planning fallacy': Why people underestimate their task completion times
claims.authors_year: Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994 (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology)
claims.url: NOT RETRIEVED - WebSearch budget exhausted before any search ran; verify by title
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran). Recalled, unverified: honours-thesis students predicted about 34 days to finish and took about 56 days; fewer than a third finished by their predicted date. No ADHD sample; an ADHD-specific test of task-time estimation in college students (Prevatt et al., 2011, Journal of Attention Disorders) exists but its direction of error is not recalled with confidence.
claims.implication: Add two numbers to each planned practice task: the student's estimate in minutes and the actual (duration_seconds already exists on practice runs). Show her a simple estimate-vs-actual line on her own view; it is both self-monitoring (C3) and time training (C8), and it is the one analytic the README's stance clearly permits because it compares her only with herself.

claims.claim: Visible countdown timers are recommended by clinical consensus for ADHD (externalising time) but this agent knows of no randomised or controlled trial of a visual timer in an ADHD sample; the closest evidence is single-case studies in which a timer or tactile prompt cues a self-monitoring check.
claims.source_title: No controlled trial known to the agent; consensus recommendation traceable to Barkley's executive-function model (ADHD and the Nature of Self-Control, 1997) and to single-case self-monitoring studies using interval prompts (e.g. Amato-Zech, Hoff & Doepke, 2006, Psychology in the Schools)
claims.url: NOT RETRIEVED - WebSearch budget exhausted before any search ran; verify by title
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran). Recalled, unverified: Amato-Zech et al. used a vibrating interval prompt (MotivAider) with three students with disabilities and reported on-task behaviour rising from roughly 55% to over 90%; not an ADHD-only sample.
claims.implication: Use a visible timer in practice blocks, but as a cue for the self-check ('timer beeps every 10 minutes: am I writing working?') rather than a pressure device; the Shooting Gallery already speeds up, so maths timers should count down calmly, not accelerate. Do not present the timer to the parent as an evidence-based intervention in its own right.

claims.source_title: A systematic review of empirical studies on learning analytics dashboards: A self-regulated learning perspective
claims.authors_year: Matcha, Uzir, Gasevic & Pardo, 2020 (IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies, 13(2))
claims.url: NOT RETRIEVED - WebSearch budget exhausted before any search ran; verify by title
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran). Recalled, unverified: 29 studies reviewed; few reported learning gains; the authors proposed a model of user-centred learning analytics giving feedback on learning processes across forethought, performance and reflection phases.
claims.implication: The parent's chart-not-leaderboard stance is consistent with this review. The student-facing view should add a forethought element ('this week: P4-P5, then A4 retest') and a one-line reflection prompt after each session, rather than only the score chart. Samples were university students, so generalisation to a 13-year-old with ADHD is untested.

claims.implication: Keep the Spanish score chart referenced to her own history plus a personal goal line (for example 80% accuracy, matching the tracker's 'secure' threshold), never to other learners or across subjects, which the README already forbids. claims.claim: In a randomised trial of STAND, a parent-teen programme in which the parent acts as coach (collaborative goal-setting, motivational interviewing, teen-chosen strategies, monitoring by agreement rather than nagging), adolescents with ADHD improved on parent-rated symptoms, organisation, homework problems and parent-teen conflict, though gains faded by follow-up and were weaker when delivered by community clinicians.
claims.source_title: Parent-teen behavior therapy + motivational interviewing for adolescents with ADHD
claims.authors_year: Sibley et al., 2016 (Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology); community effectiveness trial Sibley et al., 2021
claims.url: NOT RETRIEVED - WebSearch budget exhausted before any search ran; verify by title
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (no search ran). Recalled, unverified: 2016 trial about 128 adolescents aged 11-15 randomised to STAND (10 weekly family sessions) or treatment as usual; 2021 community trial about 278 families, with outcomes depending on clinician fidelity to motivational interviewing.
claims.implication: Give the parent a defined coaching role in the system: a short weekly co-planning meeting where the student picks from the review queue's options and sets her own targets, the parent monitors two agreed indicators (for example blanks and sessions completed as planned), and Claude's skills do the in-session enforcement. Avoid ad hoc parental running or reviewing of sessions; STAND's effect came from structured, autonomy-supporting parent involvement.

caveats: CRITICAL PROVENANCE NOTE: this session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted (200 of 200 calls) before any of this agent's 11 attempted searches ran, and WebFetch/curl are blocked by egress policy. No search result and no URL was retrieved. Every claim above is written from the agent's prior knowledge of the literature. The sources are real to the best of that knowledge, but titles, years, journals, sample sizes and effect sizes are unverified and should be treated as 'partial' at best until a verification agent checks them by title. The url fields are explicit 'NOT RETRIEVED' markers, not links, because inventing a URL would breach the no-fabrication rule.
All figures marked 'recalled, unverified' are leads for verification, not citable numbers; the instruction to quote numbers only when shown in results could not be met, so each is labelled as such.

Nothing from 2023-2026 was checked: newer meta-analyses of organisational-skills or self-management interventions in adolescents, digital self-monitoring apps, STAND follow-ups, or updated JCCAP evidence-base reviews may exist and could change the ranking in C7.

Searched-for-but-unobtainable (not searched, because of the budget): any controlled trial of visual countdown timers in ADHD (C10 reflects the agent's belief that none exists); ADHD-specific task-time-estimation studies for the planning fallacy (only general-population evidence in C9); evidence for 'weekly review' rituals as a stand-alone practice - the agent knows of none in ADHD; the weekly review is only a component of HOPS and STAND (C5, C14) and otherwise rests on productivity-method consensus.

Evidence gaps that hold regardless of verification: almost all ADHD self-regulation and organisation evidence comes from US school classrooms with teachers and peers, mostly ages 8-14; nothing is known for a home-educated 13-year-old learning largely from an AI tutor. Dashboard evidence (C12, C13) is from university students and is general-population only.

Daily report cards (C4) and most self-management studies (C3) used tangible or point rewards; whether feedback-only versions retain the effect is not established. This bears directly on the README's no-rewards stance and is flagged, not resolved.

Gawrilow's if-then studies (C1, C2) were short laboratory tasks; transfer to a 90-minute tutoring session is assumed, not demonstrated. Effects of self-monitoring (C3) are large but come mostly from single-subject designs, which inflate effect estimates relative to group RCTs.

DuPaul & Stoner ('ADHD in the Schools') was requested but is a textbook synthesis; it is referenced inside C3's implication rather than given its own claim because no trial-level number could be attributed to it.
